top.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
top.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
top.text: While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function. Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF. The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta. "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory. Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine , with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory. Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy. In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep. Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves. "You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?" To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance. Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI. Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound. The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment. The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants. The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens. By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality. The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances. This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions. "Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says. The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow. For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies. top.title: Wildfire smoke damages the airway's defenses, blocking one signal can shield them
top.summary: When the Palisades and Eaton wildfires tore through Los Angeles in January 2025, smoke blanketed the region and air quality plunged into the hazardous range. It was a vivid example of a growing problem: After years of improvement, wildfire smoke is pulling air quality back in the wrong direction, and fire season, once confined to hot, dry summers, now stretches across the year.

top.title: Alcohol, drug abuse, suicide: Is Europe really safe from America's 'deaths of despair' epidemic?
top.summary: In the United States, life expectancy diverged from Europe before it stopped rising during the 2010s, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton gave a name to a phenomenon that was then booming, partly explaining this trend: "deaths of despair," which have soared since the turn of the 21st century, especially among middle-aged white people without a college degree.

top.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
top.summary: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

top.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
top.summary: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

top.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
top.summary: Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.
top.text: Scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system. Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue. Now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles. The new battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process. To make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function. The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an important advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles. One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte. The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins. Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds. Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins." Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero. The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A , could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available. Zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs. This advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety. A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity. During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes. According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen." This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology. The successful prototype offers a new direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies. If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls. Although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles shows that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy. Materials provided by University of Córdoba . top.title: Two measures to help prevent obesity in young people
top.summary: Obesity in children and young people increases the risk of health problems later in life to such an extent that tackling it is important, both for individuals and for the population as a whole. The condition is generally linked to diet and lifestyle. A new study including almost 125,000 children examines how best to help parents and children make healthier choices. The paper is published in the journal Acta Paediatrica.

top.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
top.summary: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.

top.title: The child development 'sweet spot' that affects adult taste preference
top.summary: A baby's transition from breast milk or formula to a range of solid foods is the likely "sweet spot" for introducing nutritional variety that influences lifelong taste preferences by rewiring circuits in the brain, new research in mice suggests.

top.title: Adolescent and teen depression linked to heavier substance use
top.summary: Adolescents and teenagers who drink more alcohol or use multiple forms of marijuana are much more likely to experience major depression. In addition, girls, older teens and multiracial teens are more likely to experience major depression, regardless of drug or alcohol use.

top.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
top.summary: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

top.title: New liver model for studying alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
top.summary: AATD is a rare genetic metabolic disorder that affects the liver and lungs. A mutation causes liver cells (hepatocytes) to form misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). This misfolding results in reduced secretion of AAT into the blood plasma. AAT plays an important role in controlling inflammatory processes in the body by mitigating excessive reactions that lead to tissue damage.

top.title: A protein in the brain's immune cells may accelerate damage in Alzheimer's disease
top.summary: Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease. The study shows that galectin-3 not only influences how the brain's immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease's characteristic amyloid plaques but also shapes the plaques themselves—and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

top.title: Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
top.summary: In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).

top.title: Deadly virus reduces tree frog population by 83% in Atlantic Forest reserve
top.summary: A highly lethal pathogen is responsible for the mass death of tadpoles and the rapid decline of amphibian populations in the Atlantic Forest. A group of researchers demonstrate for the first time in South America that recurring ranavirus outbreaks caused an 83% drop in monkey frog (Phyllomedusa distincta) reproduction in a pond in the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina. The disease is caused by a virus that affects reptiles and fish as well.

top.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
top.summary: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

top.title: Whom do we expect to put others ahead of themselves: Boys or girls? New study has surprising, and unsurprising, answers
top.summary: The holiday season is a time for gatherings with family and friends—as well as for less festive but necessary duties: organizing, preparing for and cleaning up after these gatherings. These are examples of service tasks that, according to previous research, women and girls are expected to perform.

top.title: Cooking Thanksgiving dinner could create an indoor air quality problem inside your home, expert says
top.summary: The Thanksgiving turkey may be the centerpiece of the holiday meal, but cooking it, along with all the sides and other dishes, can invite an unexpected guest: indoor air pollution.

top.title: Tiny parasite holds big clues to help protect threatened estuarine turtles
top.summary: The diamondback terrapin is North America's only turtle species that lives exclusively in brackish coastal waters, such as salt marshes and estuaries. Its populations face threats from historical overharvesting and contemporary habitat loss, coastal development and accidental capture in crab traps.

top.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
top.summary: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even.

top.title: How do human lifestyles affect the gut microbiome of our canine companions?
top.summary: Dogs have been living side by side with humans for millennia, but a new study underscores how much we have yet to learn about man's best friend. The study, which looked at hundreds of dogs across four nations, found that the lifestyles of pet owners appear to play a significant role in determining what constitutes a healthy gut microbiome for their dog companions.

top.title: Strange radio signals from space could come from a dead star
top.summary: The night sky is as good a place as any for a mystery. Back in 2002, astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves coming from near the center of our galaxy, spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. The signals were detected again in 2003 and 2004, but then disappeared. Despite years of searching, there was no sign of their return.

top.title: Stem cell–derived nanoparticles modulate immune cells and help delay type 1 diabetes in mice
top.summary: In people with type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly identifies insulin-producing cells in the pancreas as foreign and attacks them, leaving the body unable to properly regulate blood sugar. While insulin therapy helps manage the disease, it does not stop the underlying immune attack.

top.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
top.summary: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

top.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
top.summary: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

top.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
top.summary: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.

top.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
top.summary: About 1 in 4 US adults are family caregivers.
top.text: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people . The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion . Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 . But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.

top.title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
top.summary: A crisis communications expert looks at how the Trump administration handled the massive disruption to the nation’s air travel when all planes were grounded on Nov. 13, 2026.
top.text: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems . Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen , a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis. The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known. A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly , in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later. You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin? He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand . And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy. By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.” How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications? They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew. However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings. We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday , all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday . Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out . But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale. If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air? What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do? To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now? How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination. They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they? It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet . So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports ? I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago , due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome ,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse. Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “ you will have more ” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them? I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop? My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th? We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.

top.title: Forms, phone calls and portals: The hidden work that keeps American institutions functioning burdens parents most
top.summary: Insurers, schools, doctors, benefits agencies – each has its own rules, databases, deadlines and definitions. Subtle misalignments compound over time, and the hassle falls heaviest on some groups.
top.text: As a working mom of three kids, I spend a lot of time parenting. I also spend a lot of time coordinating insurance, physician and school forms and remembering passwords to six different school and sports portals. None of that is really parenting, and it’s not paid work either, but it takes time away from both. I’m also a political theorist who studies how institutional design affects people’s daily lives. What many people characterize as unavoidable aspects of modern life actually provide important lessons about how various institutions are set up and who does the work to keep them functional. Most American families deal with multiple complex institutions every week: a personalized mix of health insurers and medical providers, schools, tax authorities, Social Security and benefits agencies, daycares and camps and other kid activities, and state and federal programs such as Medicaid or SNAP. Each of these programs has its own logic, including specific rules, portals, databases, forms, deadlines and definitions. This variation creates subtle misalignments across programs that compound over time. The physician needs prior authorization from the insurer, but the insurer claims the doctor needs a specific form. Meanwhile, the school needs the doctor’s document, and a benefits office might need proof that another agency already has in its system. The people working to align all these systems are parents , often people with the least time and cognitive availability to handle the burden. Political scientists Pamela Herd and Donald Moynihan of the Better Government Lab call this load administrative burden ; that burden includes learning all the rules, figuring out how to comply with them, and then handling all the rippling demands that each individual task creates. These burdens are not natural or inevitable. Instead, they’re the result of the way people have designed our institutions. The good news is that it’s possible to do things differently. Most institutions weren’t intentionally designed with the user experience in mind. Instead, they’re the result of piecemeal decisions over decades, often the result of a complex interplay of interest-group lobbying, political jockeying and public demands. Employer-based health insurance resulted, in part, from fear of socialized medicine during World War II. Public schools grew out of local communities and then had layers of state and federal regulations piled on top. Bureaucracies at different levels and of different types rarely talk to each other or bother coordinating their rules and processes. And most of these rules and processes aren’t usually nefarious in intent . Documentation can prevent fraud, eligibility rules help allocate scarce resources, regulations can protect patients, and institutions have a vested interest in protecting themselves from mistakes and liability. But each operates in isolation. The cracks are visible only to the person who has to navigate these silos – and that’s often an overextended parent. It might seem like everyone bears the same administrative burdens, but they don’t. Life administration hits some groups harder than others; women , people with disabilities and lower-income people all interact more frequently with these fragmented systems and are less able to absorb the costs of those interactions. For a middle-class American on salary, an hour on hold is a nuisance. For a waitress working for tips, it’s lost earnings or even lost employment. For many Americans, the administrative burden of applying for and proving eligibility for benefits is dramatic; the people who need these programs the most struggle to access them . This is what researchers call a regressive effect in public policy, meaning that the costs hit hardest for those who can least afford it. Many institutions are effectively means-tested in reverse: The most vulnerable pay the most in terms of time, energy and money. While there is no easy fix with institutions as complex as healthcare, education or public benefits, there are some options. One useful model is universal design : the idea that we should build our environments – in this case, institutions – for people of different abilities from the start. On the institutional front, this would mean more flexible hours to accommodate a range of users; a combination of email, phone and platform access; automatic enrollment or renewal when eligibility is already known; various plain language rules; and agencies sharing information, with permission, and working together to resolve conflicts between policies and rules so families aren’t forced into the role of unpaid institutional coordinators. Much of this will require not just language rewrites but significant investment in new systems . Michigan provides an example of reform working at scale. In 2018 the state consolidated benefit application forms across five programs, reducing length and complexity. The original combined application packet was an overwhelming 1,000 questions and over 64 pages long. The streamlined application process, which could be completed in about 20 minutes, not only improved the process for those applying. It reduced errors, cut down worker processing time and saved caseworkers 200,000 hours per year, presumably saving tax dollars along the way. Reducing administrative burden across programs is one of the few policy reforms with almost no downside. For now, many Americans are like fish swimming in polluted water. We know something’s wrong, but we can’t see the cause. The next time you’re stuck on hold trying to fix a paperwork error with one agency before you can submit additional paperwork to another, it’s worthwhile to remember that this experience isn’t an inevitability of modern life. It’s the result of design choices – or failure to make choices – that can be changed.

top.title: Florida’s flooding déjà vu is a sign of things to come – so, who is most at risk and how can they prepare?
top.summary: More than a foot of rain flooded streets in the already saturated region in mid-November 2026, with more forecast in the days ahead.
top.text: Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped more than a foot of rain in 24 hours starting Nov. 17, 2026. The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region less than three weeks earlier , and forecasters warned of more rain still to come . As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu. In April 2023, more than 25 inches of rain fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours. Even hurricanes rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast. Residents could do little to stop the flooding. Studies show that as global temperatures rise, more people will be at risk from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past. In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are low-wage workers , older adults and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves. I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an associate professor of social work . To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared. The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead as temperatures rise . These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 El Niño set in . A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture , leading to stronger downpours. The resulting deluges can be devastating. These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities continue to heat up the planet . Recent disasters show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond areas traditionally considered at risk . To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who might not be prepared . Low-lying areas with poorly planned development , lack of investment in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of historic disinvestment and discrimination are often at higher risk. So are low-income communities with tight budgets that can’t afford protective measures like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly. When older adults live in these flood-prone areas , they are at even higher risk. Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of disability that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster. They are also more likely to be socially isolated , which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering. My colleagues and I have examined how prepared people are for disasters of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role. The numbers are sobering. Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, reported they were not prepared with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck. We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education. People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters. Our research has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters. Renting adds additional challenges. In the U.S., lower-income families often depend on the rental market . They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety. And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs. The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community. That can involve investing in infrastructure , including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and strengthening the power grid , as well as ensuring that people have access to safe and affordable housing . Some communities and federal agencies have bought out properties that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way. Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among those most at risk , such as older adults and other socially marginalized groups . If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to plan for emergencies , know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike. I believe the most successful efforts are those that bring at-risk communities into planning discussions . For example, in Columbus, Ohio, the city partnered with the Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging, Age Friendly Innovation Center and my team to improve disaster preparedness among older residents . We worked with older adults in affordable housing communities and the human service professionals who support them to help design action plans for communities with special needs in the event of an emergency. The tool kit we created can help social service providers prepare low-income residents for extreme weather. Our team is now working with service providers nationwide to document best practices, identify gaps and ensure residents are better prepared for climate- and weather-related emergencies in the future.
